en: The Sutra on the Six Verses Spoken by the Buddha to the Old Woman, translated by the Tripitaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty.
The Buddha is the World-Honored One; his merit is most sublime, and out of compassion for sentient beings, he feels sorrow for them.
At that time, as he was traveling with his disciples and great beings, they came upon a place where music was being played and many teachings were being proclaimed.
There was an elderly, poor woman, hunched over from age, who knelt down and asked the Buddha:
"The five aggregates and the six sense-bases have combined to form my body; of what are they all composed?"
From where does one come?
To where does one go?
I only pray that the World-Honored One will contemplate this for me!
The Buddha said,
“Excellent! You should recognize their essential points.”
The causal conditions of all phenomena are rarely understood by those who perceive them.
It is like drilling for fire: when two pieces of wood are rubbed together, the fire does not come from the drill, nor does it come from the fire-drill itself.
Fire emerges from within it, blazing with intense brilliance, burning back its own wood until the wood is completely consumed and diminished.
It is also like beating a drum, whose sound is mournful and crushing.
Sound does not arise from the bell alone, nor does it arise from the striker alone.
All phenomena are likewise; they are produced through the mutual interaction of causes and conditions.
It is also like rain from heaven: wind, clouds, and thunder must all come together to produce rain; it is not the power of the dragon alone.
All phenomena are thus, and their designations are likewise thus.

It is like a painter who, having prepared his pigments, applies them to a surface to create a painting; there is no form that does not emerge, yet all require the convergence of conditions and do not arise through a single power alone.
Upon hearing the sutra, the woman was filled with joy and bowed deeply; she immediately attained the patience of the Dharma (dharmanidhyānakṣānti) without her body feeling any exhaustion.
Ānanda then inquired: "Who is this woman?"

He asked the Buddha, "If one inquires into the source of all dharmas and of birth and death, and thereby the mind opens and the intellect is liberated, will one immediately attain the truth of the Way?
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"Listen to what I say."
In the past, there was a Buddha named Krakucchanda.
At that time, this mother was my kinswoman.
As I practiced the Way, she clung to me and confined my body; overcome with grief and longing, she did not eat for the space of a single day.
Because of this attachment to affection, we were poor for five hundred lifetimes.
Now that I have attained Buddhahood, all myriad blessings have arrived; immeasurable sentient beings stand pure before the Buddha.
After sixty billion kalpas, he shall attain Buddhahood, named Sarva; his land shall be called Many Flowers, and the kalpa shall be named Paying Homage to Dhyāna.
At that time, the clothing and food of the people will be like those of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and each shall have a lifespan of one kalpa without any suffering or toil.
At that time, the women, devas, nāgas, and yakṣas, having heard the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, were all greatly rejoiced.
Eighty-seven thousand people attained the resolve for the right and true path, prostrated before the Buddha, and departed.
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Six Virtuous Daughters of an Old Woman.
